name: Victor Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so say what you'd tell others and what you really think. What does a working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Victor, 43, a junior developer at a tech company after a two-year college diploma. I maintain the software that checks ingredient labels for food manufacturers, and I like catching a wrong allergen word before thousands of packets are printed. I use AI every day to draft parser tests, though the senior developer still reviews the hard cases. At home my partner works at a pharmacy, and our two school-age children remind me why the mortgage comes before a new kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI saves me time on draft tests, but a packet label still has to match the ingredients on the line. I use an assistant every day to spot odd words, then compare the result with the approved recipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Under a plateau, I think my junior coding job is safe enough. My wage is high for a junior, my partner has a steady job at a pharmacy, we have ten months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of software firms close enough to reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking food-label imports and sending difficult cases to the senior developer. In the first year I'd continue using AI on sample labels, and transfer another 180 from my pay into savings each month while both wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with the usual worry that a label error can hurt somebody. AI staying modest would not change how we pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error made you change your test set?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A sample label once lost the word 'peanut' when two ingredient fields were merged. I found it before print because the approved recipe still had the word in bold; now that case is in every release test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep an old packet at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two children know why we keep the packet from that batch in a drawer. The old peanut packet reminds us that a clean screen is not the same as a safe label.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can write code, check ingredients and answer manufacturers, so junior jobs are on the line. I would rather measure wrong labels in a trial than cheer about more labels per hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be cut if the firm leaves one experienced developer to approve AI output. My savings give us time, and I am quick to learn a new tool, but I cannot assume every nearby company will be hiring juniors after the same change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run a two-month trial on old ingredient changes, tracking missed allergens and how long people spend correcting AI output. If the error rate falls, I'd learn the new approval workflow with the senior developer; in the first year we'd hold off ordering a larger kitchen until we see what happens to staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, although the trial interests me. I want the result to make labels safer, even if it raises hard questions about who gets paid to check them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which mistake must the trial catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The peanut case should be in the trial, because it looks like a tiny field merge until someone with an allergy reads the packet. If AI misses it, I'd publish the result inside the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a new checking role need to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the manager for a paid role in final label checks before taking a new title. A badge on my screen doesn't pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 could write and check our label code at once, while robots that handle factory work arrive around 2031. A family with an allergy still needs a clear person to call when a packet is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior developer wage could be cut quickly. Ten months of savings and my partner's pharmacy pay keep us from a sudden mortgage crisis, but if the whole industry buys cheap code, local software jobs may thin. A new software job may be harder than the number of local firms suggests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking food labels while collecting peanut-case evidence without customer names and ask three food plants whether they have paid label-audit posts. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to real openings whose wage with my partner's pay covers mortgage and school costs; if none exist, I'd look at other paid work while keeping the children in their current school until we have firm figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I could pay bills for a while, but I expect the coding seat I just learned to fill might vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would factory label checking stay safe once robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A plant auditor checks ingredients and printed packets on site. Robots may take more of that hands-on checking around 2031, so I would ask about actual openings and the training required, not claim it is a safe lifelong trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family defer while you search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would put the mortgage, school costs and any new wage on one page. We would not buy the larger kitchen while we are deciding which job pays next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years until 2031 gives us time to learn which factory checks really need people. Robots follow around 2034, but thinking AI reaches our label code in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn how a plant checks ingredients on the line, if someone is willing to supervise and pay for the training. My junior code work could still shrink. An audit certificate is not job security by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the quality manager to let me observe one label run each quarter if my software manager releases the time. I'd take a food-safety course only if my employer funds it and offers a paid plant-audit rotation; in the first year after 2031 I'd apply for plant posts only if paid vacancies still exist and the household wage covers mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing the coding post, but I can check the plant path without resigning. I would want to see actual work, not a training brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on a plant visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the line I'd compare the ingredient sheet with a printed packet and ask who stops the run if they differ. I would not touch production controls before being trained and authorised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner ask about the rotation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would ask whether the rotation keeps my salary and gives a named supervisor. If it does not, I would keep my software wage and ask other plants about real vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years to 2036 gives companies time to keep a record of which labels failed and who fixed them. Thinking AI reaches our code in 2036, with hands-on factory robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I could be paid to check labels on site, or I could be looking for work. For the next few years our two wages and ten-month cushion feel secure, but no one can promise a plant will still want a human checker after 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a record of ingredient errors I caught, including the peanut case, without names or private recipes. We'd save 180 monthly while both wages hold, and I would take funded food-safety training only if a paid plant rotation is offered; in the first year after 2036 I'd switch only for a signed plant or software role covering mortgage and school costs with my partner's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, curious about how plant work changes. I can keep learning without gambling the mortgage on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be in your record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My record would show the field merge that dropped 'peanut' and the test that caught it. A future employer can judge my label checks without seeing a customer's recipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about future training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children may want to work with machines one day. I'd suggest a paid apprenticeship with real supervision if one exists, then let them decide what they want to learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because both coding and checking could cheapen before I have a paid alternative. A notice period, real plant-audit vacancies and training linked to paid supervised work would help us use savings wisely.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who answers when a printed packet harms someone. A manufacturer cannot send a corrected code file to a family with an allergic child; a person must explain and fix the label.

headlineQuote: A manufacturer cannot send a corrected code file to a family with an allergic child; a person must explain and fix the label.
portrait: Victor, **43**, is a junior food-label developer with a two-year diploma who tests ingredient words against approved recipes.
His **higher pay**, partner's pharmacy wage, ten-month cushion and many nearby software firms support a mortgage and two children.
He uses AI **daily** for tests but caught a missing peanut word before printing.
Steady disruption makes him **anxious** about junior cuts; 2028 AGI alarms him despite strong savings.
With more time, he seeks **paid plant-audit learning**, funding and signed jobs covering family bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove both junior coding and checking work before he finds a paid alternative.
whatWouldHelp: A **notice period**, real plant-audit vacancies and funded supervised training would help.
